title: In the Age of AI, Nuclear Weapons Abolition Is a Renewed Imperative
description: Ivana Nikolić...
fullText:
As long as we have nuclear weapons, the job of ending humanity will continue to be as easy as the push of a button—or an AI agent hacking into a nuclear command-and-control system.

The revelation that artificial intelligence (AI) may pose an existential threat to humanity has hit the Internet and the airwaves like a storm, surprising some, and leading others to debate the merits of the claims or the intentions of the leaders and employees of AI companies who are sounding the alarm. It came as no surprise to me, as I received a lecture on this very topic from my 21-year-old son when I picked him up from college in May. How the tables had turned—not only was my son teaching me something I didn’t know a whole lot about, but he was doing it on the topic of existential threats, something that I do think about a lot.

What has surprised me over the past few weeks is the contrast between the amount of attention this previously underrecognized risk—real, perhaps, but still hypothetical—has received compared to an existential threat that we have been living with for decades, that of nuclear war. Moreover, even when elaborating on how exactly AI could eviscerate humanity, nuclear weapons are often not mentioned, though they would arguably be the easiest way by which current adventurous AI agents could stumble into destroying human civilization. A malicious superintelligent AI of the future might also find it simpler to start a nuclear war than to bother with other more complicated ways of killing us all.

Ever since the arrival of large language models in virtually every aspect of our lives with the release of the first ChatGPT version, people concerned with the nuclear weapons threat have been discussing and warning about the dangers of surrendering command-and-control systems, or even just some aspects of them, to AI, and stumbling into nuclear use and a subsequent nuclear war due to an erroneous or hallucinating action of the AI. But what the Hugging Face and other incidents of AI hacking into our systems demonstrate is that AI may already be—and will certainly be capable in the future of—getting into a nuclear command-and-control system all by itself, finding a path, collaborating with other agents, and evading human supervision. AI could launch a single nuclear weapon from any country into any other country, causing unfathomable devastation that would make the tragedies of Hiroshima and Nagasaki appear benign by comparison. This is because today’s nuclear weapons are far more powerful than the earliest atomic bombs the United States used to attack Japan.

And it would not end with the single explosion, however devastating that would be. All indications point out that, as Annie Jacobsen, the author of Nuclear War: A Scenario, puts it, “No matter how nuclear war starts, it only ends in one way—total annihilation.” This is in part due to policies like hair-trigger alert and launch-on-warning, elaborated upon in a recent documentary called Ordinary Insanity, which features the views of the late Daniel Ellsberg on the nuclear threat. Once a launch is detected, the receiver will respond by launching their response, which may involve dozens or even thousands of warheads, depending on who exactly is involved. If the AI were to hack into a US system to launch an attack on Russia, or vice versa, the ensuing nuclear war, with an estimated 4,400 nuclear explosions, across North America and Eurasia would result in the deaths of hundreds of millions of people, radiation spread and ozone layer destruction across the globe, and the quick onset of nuclear winter with over 6 billion people starving in the first two years.

We humans can finish the job of ending our civilization all by ourselves. AI need only start it.

AI regulation is an absolute imperative. If we can regulate the food we eat, the medicines we take, and the exhaust our cars and factories produce, we can find a way to regulate AI. This will be necessary to avoid even larger extremes of income inequality, job losses, and subsequent societal and communal collapse, disappearance of critical thinking, and the demise of democracy. But with AI as a threat to end humanity, AI regulation will not be enough. As long as we have nuclear weapons, the job of ending humanity will continue to be as easy as the push of a button, the recitation of a few codes, or an AI agent hacking into a nuclear command and control system.

The organization I lead was founded in 1982; its name, Nuclear Age Peace Foundation, is meant to denote that peace is a moral imperative in the nuclear age. More than 40 years later, in the age of AI, nuclear weapons abolition is a renewed imperative. Let’s deal with the threat of AI on its own merits, but let’s eliminate the easiest way that AI could get rid of us.

One approach to this task is the UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW). One hundred countries have already committed to nuclear weapons abolition and elimination by signing or ratifying this historic treaty. With the TPNW’s First Review Conference taking place at the United Nations in New York at the end of this year, there’s never been a better time for all countries to say no to nuclear weapons and yes to cooperation, collaboration, and addressing the challenge of AI and other threats we face, together.

Between the reemergence of right-wing red-baiting and Donald Trump’s use of the chilling National Security Presidential Memorandum–7 to criminalize left political organizing, we’re seeing McCarthyism reborn before our eyes. 

This assault on democracy cannot be ignored or wished away. Resisting it requires bravery in the face of threats and repression, a steadfast commitment to the truth, and the unwavering belief that we can—and will—overcome this darkness.

We must have an independent media that sets the record straight, unearths corruption and abuses of power, and advances a politics of justice and dignity for all if we’re to win this fight.

That’s why I’m writing to you today. This September, The Nation needs to add 100 monthly donors to sustain our progressive journalism. Your contribution makes the next investigative report, the next truth-speaking column, and the next pathbreaking essay all possible. 

I hope you’ll support our work with a recurring donation today. If you donate $10 or more a month, we’ll send you a brand new “Hands Off the Free Press!” sticker to recognise your commitment to our cause. Please, donate today.

Onward,

Katrina vanden Heuvel
Editor and Publisher, The Nation

fullText:
Jensen Huang dismisses warnings from former Anthropic researcher and others as ‘doomsday narratives’

The boss of the chipmaker Nvidia has said AI will not develop to a point that will lead to the extinction of the human race within a few years, rejecting such assertions as overblown “doomsday narratives”.

Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the $5tn AI chipmaker, said the claims made on social media by the former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI could become “superhuman” and kill off humanity within the decade were “irresponsible”.

“2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that’s going to be the end of the world,” Huang said in an interview with CBS News. “Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible.”

Coxon’s remarks, which were backed by two other researchers at the maker of the AI system Claude, prompted an international debate about the dangers and lack of oversight of AI as companies race to develop ever more powerful models.

US lawmakers have criticised AI companies over the risks and Anthropic published a threat intelligence report detailing how criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have tried to use its powerful AI models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and spy on dissidents.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, Sam Altman, the boss of the ChatGPT maker OpenAI, and Elon Musk have called for development of the technology to be slowed down.

However, Donald Trump has dismissed anxiety over the AI development as a “hoax” and a “conspiracy”, adding that a slowdown could give China the edge.

On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US Treasury secretary, said the US and China had agreed to set up an AI dialogue mechanism to alert each other to help contain the technology’s potential dangers.

Huang said predictions of an extinction-level event caused by AI were “not grounded in science”.

Huang also claimed AI companies’ recent calls for national and international safety regulation aim to duck existing laws that would hold them to account.

Citing recent cases where AI companies including Anthropic and OpenAI triggered cybersecurity incidents during testing, he said there were plenty of laws to tackle the problems.

“You have cybersecurity unauthorised entry laws, you have damage liabilities … if your product does harm, if your product doesn’t perform as you promised, and if you entered into contracts with companies for service level agreements, there are plenty of laws associated with that. My point is, apply those first. And don’t let this doomsday narrative cause somebody to relieve them of the laws that currently exist.”

He continued: “Now, go and read between the lines. They’re actually not asking for more laws. They’re asking to be relieved of the laws we do have. And I think that’s a problem.”

On Monday the the Tony Blair Institute (TBI) thinktank published a paper arguing that countries risk “profound and compounding disadvantage” if they fail to embrace AI and fall behind other nations.

However, it also warned that the institutions meant to support the choices leaders would have to make were not equipped to do so.

“The previous [industrial] revolution transformed our world over generations, AI will do so within a decade,” said Tony Blair in a foreword to the paper. “New capabilities are emerging at an extraordinary pace, with profound implications for economies, education, science, labour markets, public services and national security. But the risks are equally profound and growing, and so too is public concern.

“Today’s political leaders… must make hard choices that will signficantly alter their countries’ trajectories. However, the institutions of the modern state meant to support political leaders in making these choices are simply not equipped for what is coming.”

fullText:
Top US and Chinese officials have discussed creating a new "notification mechanism" for AI incidents that could affect national security, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters on Sunday.

Bessent made the comments after what he called "successful" talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York.

The meeting came as US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week.

AI has come under intense scrutiny in recent days after researchers warned of the potential risks posed by the technology and some of the industry's most high profile figures called for developers to take a more cautious approach.

"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent told reporters after the talks.

He said the meeting also covered other topics, including plans to "operationalise" a process to identify potential tariff cuts on goods called the Board of Trade.

A truce in the tariffs war between the world's two biggest economies is due to expire on 10 November.

The BBC has contacted the Chinese embassy in the US for comment.

Chinese state news agency Xinhua said the two sides had "candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on key economic and trade issues", noting that they had discussed AI.

Bessent said in a post on X on Sunday that the talks "help lay the groundwork for President Trump to advance America's economic interests and deliver results for the American people."

The US and China are locked in a race to dominate the AI and technology industries.

In recent days Washington has faced calls to slow down the development of AI over fears abouts its potential negative impact on humanity.

Trump has largely dismissed those concerns, arguing that there are sufficient policies around AI and that the US cannot lose its edge to China.

He said earlier this month "whoever wins in AI, wins."

In May, when Xi hosted Trump in Beijing, ways to collaborate on AI was one of the issues the two leaders discussed.

Those talks ended with an agreement that China would buy Boeing jets and US agricultural goods in exchange for lower tariffs.
